analysis.one_liner: Bars the FTC from using its own informal guidance as the basis for enforcement actions against companies.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors and never advanced beyond a House subcommittee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Federal Trade Commission Act so the FTC could not bring or settle an enforcement action based only on its guidelines, policy statements, or similar guidance — it would have to prove an actual violation of law. Companies accused of breaking FTC-enforced rules could then point to the agency's own guidance as evidence that they complied. Supporters of such limits argue businesses should not be penalized for conduct the agency never formally wrote into law; consumer advocates worry it would strip the FTC of a flexible tool it uses to police deceptive advertising, data misuse, and other unfair practices.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing FTC enforcement — including large tech platforms, advertisers, and consumer-facing financial firms — would gain a new defense: compliance with the FTC's own guidance could be offered as evidence they obeyed the law, and the agency could no longer build cases on informal policy statements alone.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the FTC, in any enforcement action, to prove a violation of a provision of law it enforces, and bars the agency from basing an enforcement action or consent order on conduct that is merely 'inconsistent' with FTC guidance unless it also violates actual law [S2] [S3].
It states that no FTC guideline or policy statement confers rights on anyone or binds the FTC or any person, state, or locality to the approach it recommends [S2] [S3].

It lets a defendant in an FTC enforcement action offer the agency's guidelines or policy statements as evidence of compliance with the law, strengthening companies' ability to defend themselves [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers would bear the cost if enforcement weakens: the FTC's informal guidance is how it has often signaled and pursued action on deceptive advertising, data misuse, and unfair practices, and a narrower agency would mean less protection from such conduct.

drawbacks.text: The FTC has sometimes treated its own guidance as if it carried legal force, and businesses can face pressure to comply with policy statements that were never formally adopted as rules — the bill responds to that due-process concern by requiring the agency to prove a real violation of law [S2] [S3].

The cost of that protection falls on the public: many FTC actions targeting deceptive or unfair practices rest on the agency's guidance documents, and the bill would bar the FTC from proceeding on that basis alone, leaving fewer tools against conduct the law has not yet spelled out in detail [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a fair due-process argument that businesses should not be sanctioned based on informal guidance the agency never wrote into law. But the FTC's guidance is also one of its main tools for policing quickly evolving practices like online data misuse and deceptive advertising, and this bill would have taken that tool largely off the table. Because the bill died without action, neither the shield nor the cost ever materialized.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no further action before Congress ended [S1] [S5] [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Kelly Armstrong introduced the bill on April 20, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, and no markup, vote, or further action followed [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are no worse off: the FTC's existing enforcement authority, including its ability to act on guidance-based cases, remained intact because the bill never became law. No industry gained the new defense it would have created.

for.name: Rep. Kelly Armstrong
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee; pursued no cosponsors during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No committee action, floor vote, or cosponsors ever materialized, so no party split is visible in the record; the bill was a single Republican member's effort with no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Companies under FTC enforcement (tech platforms, advertisers, data-driven consumer businesses)
industries.note: Had the bill passed, these companies could not be charged based on FTC guidance alone and could offer compliance with that guidance as evidence of innocence. Its interest runs against consumers in FTC-adversarial cases, since a weakened agency means less recourse for deceptive advertising or data misuse. The bill died, so no gain occurred [S2] [S3].

The bill would narrow the agency's ability to base enforcement actions and consent orders on informal guidance, a tool it uses to police unfair and deceptive practices. It would have left the FTC with fewer options against conduct not yet codified in law. Nothing was lost because the bill never advanced [S2] [S3].
